# 017 · A hybrid logical clock rewritten with max(), proved to never go backwards on any input

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✓ Verified: property holds on every input** | functional, no-false-positive | none | refactor, behaviour change not intended | [`HybridLogicalClock#receive`](../../../examples/demo/apps/quorum/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/quorum/clock/HybridLogicalClock.java) | [B11: Property proofs](../../../lib/README.md) |

> The receive rule of a hybrid logical clock has four branches; a developer rewrites it as one `max` and two conditionals. The property the clock exists for, that the new timestamp is later than both the last one and the message's and never behind the physical clock, is proved for every pair of 64-bit timestamps and every wall-clock reading. The refactor is merged on the strength of the proof, not of a review of the branches.

## The change

Compute the physical part as the maximum of the three physical parts, then derive the counter: continue the last timestamp's counter if the last timestamp had that physical part, and take the larger of that and the message's counter if the message had it too. The four-way branch becomes three lines.

**Before** ([`HybridLogicalClock.java`](../../../examples/demo/apps/quorum/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/quorum/clock/HybridLogicalClock.java), line 55):

```java

    /** The timestamp of a receive event, given the message's timestamp. */
    public static long receive(long nowMillis, long last, long message) {
        long lastPhysical = physical(last);
        long messagePhysical = physical(message);
        if (nowMillis > lastPhysical && nowMillis > messagePhysical) {
            return of(nowMillis, 0);
        }
        if (lastPhysical == messagePhysical) {
            return of(lastPhysical, Math.max(logical(last), logical(message)) + 1L);
        }
        if (lastPhysical > messagePhysical) {
            return of(lastPhysical, logical(last) + 1L);
        }
        return of(messagePhysical, logical(message) + 1L);
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java

    /** The timestamp of a receive event, given the message's timestamp. */
    public static long receive(long nowMillis, long last, long message) {
        long physical = Math.max(nowMillis, Math.max(physical(last), physical(message)));
        long logical = 0;
        if (physical == physical(last)) {
            logical = logical(last) + 1L;
        }
        if (physical == physical(message)) {
            logical = Math.max(logical, logical(message) + 1L);
        }
        return of(physical, logical);
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

The method returns without throwing and `result > last && result > message && (result >>> 16) >= nowMillis && result == receive(nowMillis, message, last)` holds on every input where `nowMillis >= 0 && nowMillis <= 0x7FFFFFFFFFFFL && last >= 0 && message >= 0 && (last & 0xFFFF) < 0xFFFF && (message & 0xFFFF) < 0xFFFF` holds.

This is a proof over the whole domain (nowMillis: long × last: long × message: long), not a sample. JBMC turned the statement into a satisfiability problem over the bytecode and showed that it has no solution: no input violates the property.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Every existing unit test passes, as it should (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.quorum.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

None, and that is the point: a verifier that only fails builds is switched off. The receive rule is the one place where two clocks and a wall clock meet, the kind of code a reviewer re-derives by hand with a table of cases. Here the table is the prover's job. The properties in the file are the ones the paper proves for the algorithm (the clock is monotonic and stays within the physical clock's drift), and the proof covers the 2^47 physical values, the 2^16 counters and every combination of them, which no test and no review does.

## Why the verdict is right

The properties file states, for `receive`: on every input with a valid wall-clock reading and two well-formed timestamps whose counters are not exhausted, the result is greater than the last timestamp and the message's, its physical part is at least the wall clock, and it equals `receive(nowMillis, message, last)`, since the rule must not care which of the two timestamps is called "last". The last clause is a law stated by calling the method inside its own property. JBMC proves all of it over the three `long` parameters in about a second. For an equivalence-preserving refactor this is exactly the assurance wanted: the new code has the properties the old code was proved to have. (Example 018 is the same refactor with one case dropped, which the same property refutes.)

## What to do

Merge. The properties did not change, so the pull request contains code only, and the proof is re-run on every build.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: JBMC 6.11.0: 2 properties proved over nowMillis: long × last: long × message: long in 0.9 s; loops unwound 16 times with unwinding assertions.

        assert e == 0 && (result > last && result > message && (result >>> 16) >= nowMillis && result == net.terminalvalue.quorum.clock.HybridLogicalClock.receive(nowMillis, message, last)); // no exception, and the property
